messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At sixty-seven, Arthur Vance was walking from the service entrance of his hotel when a man stepped out from behind a delivery bay. The assailant’s breath carried a sharp, sour reek of cheap liquor, and before Arthur could step back, a loud, metallic clatter echoed as the man dropped his keys and lunged forward. He demanded Arthur’s wallet and signet ring at knifepoint, his posture rigid and erratic, leaving Arthur frozen on the damp asphalt. The man fled as quickly as he had appeared, leaving Arthur alone in the dim parking lot with his racing heart and the lingering stench of alcohol. In the weeks that followed, Arthur’s interpretation of the attack hardened into a rigid framework. He had come to believe that people can't be trusted and that the world is a dangerous place where decent men are routinely picked apart by unseen predators. He also felt permanently humiliated by what happened, replaying his own paralyzed compliance as a profound personal failure. Because these beliefs took root so deeply, his nervous system never settled; the conviction that danger was omnipresent and that his own judgment was fundamentally flawed kept him locked in a state of perpetual threat. He found himself being superalert or watchful or on guard at all hours, his muscles coiled tight, convinced that another attacker could materialize without warning. This constant state of high alert directly shaped how his senses began to filter the world. Because he remained in a permanent state of defensive scanning, ordinary environmental cues were instantly flagged as potential danger. At the front desk of the hotel he managed, the faint whiff of alcohol from a late-checking guest’s coat collar sent his pulse racing. He would fixate on housekeeping staff moving through the service corridors, reading every shifted shoulder or lingering glance as people acting suspiciously. Even a dropped luggage cart in the lobby triggered an immediate auditory shock, the sudden loud noises mirroring the keys that had clattered on the night of the attack. His body had learned to treat these sensory details as precise coordinates for threat. Now, the fatigue of maintaining this watch continues to dictate his days. In his hotel office, he spends his mornings pacing the perimeter of the room, checking the locks twice, unable to sit with his back to the door. The feeling of being on guard even inside his own home follows him through his bedroom and kitchen. When his wife, Elena, reaches over to adjust his collar or tap his shoulder during dinner, he reacts with alarm when someone touches him unexpectedly, his hand snapping up to block the contact. He no longer parks in the hotel lot. He has stopped attending evening staff functions. The cycle tightens with each passing week, his nervous system refusing to let him stay after dark. Arthur is here because the exhaustion of maintaining this watch is finally outpacing his ability to compensate. He has come to the clinic after months of rising blood pressure, a trembling hand that makes signing the nightly reports impossible, and Elena’s quiet warning that he is becoming a stranger in his own house. He hopes for a way to quiet the internal siren, to stop reading every shadow as a prelude to violence, and to believe that he can walk through his own lobby without bracing for the blow that he knows, deep down, is no longer coming.
